speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR POLICY STATEMENT ON NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order, please. I understand that the hon. member is not moving his motion now but simply giving notice of his intention to move the motion at the end of his speech.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR POLICY STATEMENT ON NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; and to give the various parties an opportunity to see what the motion is.
I mentioned in my opening remarks that the government has tended within the last four years to go from crisis to crisis, and I intend to develop at some length the crisis we are talking about now because there is a clear cut case for a decision here which cannot be left until tomorrow or the next day. This decision must be made immediately.
In respect of some of the policy statements listed in this motion there is an urgency for something to be done as soon as possible. I intend to demonstrate that as a result of studies already completed or in the process of being completed we have enough information to make these policy statements possible. I intend to point out that because of the delay
October 23, 1367

in making these policy statements we are perhaps unwittingly, though in some cases, I am tempted to say knowingly and deliberately, leaving our country in danger of losing valuable resources, and setting precedents that we will not be able to easily change.
For instance, to show the confusion which exists I should like to read from a newspaper clipping I hold in my hand dated October 18 of last week. This is from the Globe and Mail and the headline is "Marchand asks unity to fight U.S. domination." Under a Canadian Press heading the clipping then continues in part as follows:
The power of the U.S. economy weighs on English and French speaking Canadians alike and should be faced by a united Canadian front, manpower minister Jean Marchand said yesterday.
The article continues later as follows:
"But we don't have the $10 billion that could give us, even if we had the talent for it, an equal economy and technology of our own.
What we must do is see things as they are-not tear one another apart but see if we can find a way together. Maybe together we have a chance to do something about it."
Quebec is not alone in the fear of overwhelming U.S. economic domination. He said "The Anglo Canadians have the same problem we do."
I read that statement into the record to indicate the theme of what I am going to say today. We tried last week when this crisis came to a head to find out from the minister responsible what guidance the minister and the government were going to give the National Energy Board now engaged in this confrontation with the federal power commission in Washington. Last October 19 I asked this question in the house:
-my question is addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of the direct challenge by the United States federal power commission to the principals of the National Energy Board Act and the recommendation of the Borden royal commission that we should not subsidize United States consumers of gas at the expense of Canadians, will the government make a statement of policy before the National Energy Board opens hearings next Thursday on the new application of Westcoast Transmission Company for the export of additional natural gas to the United States?
The minister who is supposed to be on top of things in order to help the Canadian people defend their interests made this reply:
Mr. Speaker, I may be wrong but I think the Westcoast case is already before the National Energy Board. However, may X take notice of the question and answer it more properly tomorrow.
The next day passed but there was no statement. Let me go on to say that this warning of what the government is leading us into is not new. If the records of this
Policy Statement on National Resources house over the last four years were searched I am sure you would find that two or three times a year I have asked the government what it was doing about giving some clear direction vis-a-vis the United States and Canada about handling the energy resouces of this continent. I have asked this over and over again but no answer has been given, except that the government will make a statement at some time in the future or it does not think it is ready to make a statement yet, but in every case there has been evasion with no action.
Last year, for example, on June 15, this statement appeared in the Ottawa Citizen under the heading "Canada's Resources- Hamilton Seeks Clear Policy To Avoid Trouble". Let me read part of that article in the local newspaper which should be a guide to all members of the government opposite. It states:
Trouble will develop between the National Energy Board of Canada and the U.S. federal power commission unless the government sets out a clear policy on resource development.
Alvin Hamilton, former Conservative agriculture minister, warned Wednesday in the commons.
The MP for Qu'Appelle, Sask., a Conservative leadership candidate and a staunch defender of Canadian autonomy, also called for a policy statement on a national hydro-electric transmission grid.
He said such a grid is "vital to the whole concept of sovereignty and using our energy as a basic part of strengthening our bargaining power in the field of resource use on the continent."
Mr. Hamilton threw a barrage of questions at Energy Minister Pepin as the minister introduced the $142,000,000 spending estimates for the energy, mines and resources department for the 1967-68 fiscal year.
He did not specify in what area he felt trouble might arise between the energy board and power commission but said he had been waiting four years for the government to outline its policy on oil and gas transmission, oil and gas regulations in the north and on the continental shelf, the relationship between atomic electric power and hydro resources and a national water policy which "we desperately need."
I will not read the whole statement. Every time the house rules have given me an opportunity I have tried to let the government know that we expect it to take the lead in defending Canadian interests because of the fact that the two great nations on this continent are struggling for the control and use of the tremendous resources of this country Canada. This struggle can be documented in many ways. There are at least three reports available to the United States government about the necessity of their industrialists and their entrepreneurs gaining access to these resources in Mexico, in Canada and all over
Ociober 23, 1967

Policy Statement on National Resources the world. With their industrialists warning their legislators and their administrators of what must be done, surely it is in our interests here in Canada to likewise have some clearcut knowledge of where we are going.
What I have said in a very general way about this question of the need for resource policies for Canada applies in particular to things like the natural gas fields, which I will deal with in a few minutes, and national oil resources. We stated a national oil policy in the house in 1961. We set targets each year until the end of 1963. The industry met those targets on the clearcut principles we established at that time, namely that our producers of oil had the right to efficiency of production equivalent to those of the United States. We were setting out to achieve production to meet not only our demands in Canada but also our exports to the United States, equal to our imports into the Montreal market.
That clearcut statement of government policy achieved almost to a barrel the results that we asked for without any form of harm to the producers in the United States. All this did was give fair play to our producers in Canada and the chance to get equality of opportunity and participation in the development of resources on this continent. We are carrying a load under our national oil policy in respect of importation of oil from Venezuela, as we should as part of the community of world nations with some responsibility to others. We expect the United States to carry part of that load as well at the receiving end in their country in respect of a number of barrels each year equivalent to our importation into Montreal.
New targets have not been set, and I say it is in the interests not only of the producers of oil but of the whole country, and the economy of our nation demands it, that some solution be stated. This can be stated unilaterally. There is no need to do anything more than inform the United States government of what we are doing. These are our resources. That government moves in the interests of their producers and naturally they expect our government to move in the interests of our producers.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
At first when this government took over, in 1963-64, there was evidence that it believed along these lines and accepted the position our government had taken in the years from 1957 to 1962. But in the last three years, under pressure from the United States, there has been a complete retreat from these positions. That is why we go from crisis to crisis.

The crisis we are now in is a clearcut challenge, as I shall demonstrate, to not only the National Energy Board but to the government and the people of Canada by the federal power commission.
I could outline the need for a policy on all these fronts, but do not take my word alone for it. In April, 1966 one of the few Canadians who has been able to survive in the development of oil and gas in our country, Mr. R. A. Brown Jr., president of Home Oil Company urged-and I quote from the Globe and Mail of April 26, 1966-that the federal government take another, hard look at our national oil policy. He said he questioned very seriously whether in its present form it was adequate to fill the needs of the Canadian oil industry or the Canadian economy. I could read the whole article.
Other submissions have come to the government and members of the opposition from various sectors of the industry. The Monetary Times in September, 1966 repeated this demand. It said we needed a new oil policy in this country. Figures were given to substantiate this statement. But the criteria we laid down in 1961 are not being followed. There is much evidence, going back for years, of the need for a simple statement in this respect. The government does not need to study this question any more because the facts are there in the royal commission report of 1957 and 1958 and in the report of the Borden royal commission.
The minister responsible in those early days, now the Minister of Finance, accepted that report and in a speech praised it as one of the great monuments of the Conservative government. That government laid down the conditions, directions and guide lines, and the Minister of Finance said his government would follow them. Where has all that resolution gone? Just as we have lacked a clearcut national policy in respect of oil, so do we lack such a policy in respect of water, agriculture, forestry, fisheries and even on that vital subject of securities.
Over and over again in the house and in meetings between the legislators of the United States and Canada we have asked the question, what are we going to do about bringing in a rule of law as between the United States institution, the securities exchange commission, and our soon to be established national exchange institution in Canada? We must have some form of direction and rule by which we can handle the joint problems we have with closely associated countries on the issue of securities.
October 23, 1967

Over and over again no action is taken until we are in a crisis. We had the crisis of last year and the one of the year before dealing with the breakdown of some of our companies in eastern Canada. In respect of a policy for water, agriculture, forestry, fisheries and securities we have the information now, there is no need to delay making these statements.
We do not need definitive statements to the last decimal point. We need statements that will let the various agencies which look after these matters, and the private companies who bargain with each other, know what are the rules of the game. They will follow these rules if they are given direction. Therefore my point in introducing this subject is to make clear the need for immediate statements in respect of these policies. We need to make absolutely clear that we face a crisis in this regard.
I will give some of the details, but before doing so I would say that, speaking now as a politician, the thing that strikes me as completely hopeless about the whole situation is that in the last four years the government has had time to deal with any number of subjects, each one important in itself but not as important as building an economic base on which we can afford all these things.
We have spent hours discussing bicultural-ism, bilingualism, the constitution, abortion, capital punishment, which was dealt with more than once, and divorce. Elections we have time for. Patronage we have time for. We have time for patronage when people are looking for jobs after they leave a sinking ship. We have spent hours in the house discussing these matters. These subjects are important, but the really important thing in Canada and in any country is to make sure that the economic base is strengthened and expanded. There must be equality of opportunity by regions.
Of course in this whole concept of building the economic strength of Canada the key is energy. This is one thing we have. We have natural gas, oil, uranium and electricity from several sources. We have energy in our tar sands. All these sources of energy, together with coal and of course uranium, are the key to power, economically, for any nation in the future. All I am asking in this motion today is that Liberals as well as the N.D.P., Credi-tistes and Conservatives forget their partisanship for a moment and simply ask the government to state the obvious.

Policy Statement on National Resources
I intend during these remarks to use as an example in the current crisis what I call the Westcoast Transmission story. Many members of the house may not recall that the discovery of large quantities of petroleum or fossil fuels has come about in the last 20 years in Canada. In order to get sufficient capital to keep the exploration going it is necessary to build pipe lines to carry the results of previous exploration into the homes of consumers. In 1952 a Canadian company, which we will call Westcoast, began to make moves to collect capital in order to build a pipe line from the Peace River area of Alberta and British Columbia, down through the mountains to Vancouver.
In order to make this pipe line economic it was necessary to have some exportation of gas into the United States. Let me read this story to the serious minded members of the house. I take the story from the first report of the royal commission on energy, dated October, 1958. If any person wants to look up the references I shall be quoting from page 14 to page 27 of that report.
Here is the story. This company applied to the federal power commission of the United States for permission to export. In June, 1954 the application to export into the United States was denied by the federal power commission on the grounds that the American federal power commission, representing all the American people, wanted to preserve the security of the American nation by making certain that every part of the United States would be supplied, if at all possible, from American sources of gas rather than from foreign sources.
Here we have an example of an agency of a foreign government protecting the interests of the producers and consumers of their country. I would say in all fairness, as a nationalist myself, that I think this was a legitimate type of thing for the federal power commission to do. In December of 1954 agreement was reached that the company which obtained the licence to distribute gas in this area, and which got a supply up from the San Juan valley in New Mexico, could import a little gas from Canada. This permission was obtained from the F.P.C.
Here is the key fact. This particular company in the United States, knowing that the Canadian company, Westcoast, had to have a certain amount of gas sales beyond its borders to make the pipe line economic and in order that they could borrow the money with which to build the pipe line, put the boots to the Canadian company and said "All we will
Ociober 23, 1967

Policy Statement on National Resources street and says "I am ready for anyone". He meets the good guy and the good guy has to decide whether he steps out into the wide street to shoot it out.
These words "high noon" are not my words, Mr. Speaker. I should like to read to the house-indeed I hope to all people in Canada-what one American, one of the commissioners of the federal power commission, said in a minority report. These words "high noon" are the words of a responsible commissioner who is trying to advise the United States government what action it should take. He disagreed with the decision that was handed down last month and had this to say, as reported by the Vancouver Sun on September 30:
The commission ... candidly serves notice upon Canada that its gas will be accepted at the international boundary only if Canadian sellers, whether before the commission or not, adhere to the American regulatory framework.
How do you like those words, Mr. Speaker? We in Canada can sell gas only if we accept direction on the matter of prices by the United States federal power commission. These are the words of a commissioner of the F.P.C. in the United States, not the words of a Canadian. The report I have of his remarks goes on:
He noted that the N.E.B. "virtually required the Canadian supplier to recoup for the Canadian economy the presumed lost benefits of the 22-cent rate."
Why should not the National Energy Board obey Canadian law and the recommendations of a royal commission? After all, Mr. Speaker, they are there to defend Canadian interests. The report continues:
Between the Federal Power Commission and the Canadian regulatory counterpart, today's (FPC) opinion says, it is "high noon". The commission apparently expects the Canadian energy board to concede to the federal Power Commission the larger role over border transactions. The premise is that the federal regulators can negotiate a better deal for the United States than Canadian regulators can negotiate for Canada.
This is not the case for such a confrontation ... If security considerations are not present, then our questions about a proposed import ought to start with whether on straight economic considerations the Canadian volumes are cheaper than the best available alternative domestically.
What is the meaning of the last part of that statement, Mr. Speaker? Commissioner Carver of the federal power commission was objecting in his minority report to the majority view of the federal power commission which is trying to take unto itself the right to decide on energy in North America. He is a loyal-thinking American. He knows that if

the United States gets into a tight with Canada over energy the United States has no bargaining power. He knows that the United States government has before it three major reports, the most scientific reports they can compile, on the future oil, gas, and energy demands and supplies in the United States. The Paley report of 1952, the Netschert report of 1958 and the Landsberg report of 1963 all pointed out that the year of crisis in the United States for the supply of natural gas is 1970.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the bargaining power in this regard is all on the side of Westcoast Transmission Co. Limited. In the normal course of business the F.P.C. did not interfere in the matter of price in 1954 when the Canadian company was being gored and there was no Canadian body to protect it. But now equality and equity are coming back into the negotiations. The bargaining power is coming over to our side and we now have a National Energy Board to see that Canadian interests are protected.
I repeat that the federal power commission has gone beyond its terms of reference, terms that one would think a nationalist institution of that kind would naturally follow. The United States is now going to have to pay an economic rate, which is just a fraction of a cent different from that at Vancouver, and the federal power commission is going to start a shoot-out.
Put yourself, Mr. Speaker, in the position of the Canadian company which is trying to sell some of the gas reserves that are being developed in the Peace River area. Put yourself in the place of the National Energy Board which has had no direction from the government. Neither the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) nor any minister has stood up and stated what the Canadian people believe, and as I say we are now faced with a shoot-out.
I say this because a third proposal is now before the National Energy Board which seeks to retain this new low price of 29.5 cents for the new quantities to be supplied and asks for a continuation of the subsidizing of United States consumers of gas by Canadian consumers under the old agreement, as has been the case for the last 12 years. All of the costs involved in maintaining the pipe line have been paid by Canadians, and we are now being asked to continue this subsidy.
I have not related all of the grim story, Mr. Speaker. In 1954, when it was thought that the Canadian company was doomed because its proposal in the spring had been
October 23, 19G7

turned down for the first time by the federal power commission, the United States company demanded, in addition to greater control over the purchase of a smaller amount of gas, that the Canadian company turn over 50 per cent of the ownership in the company to the United States company. This was not agreed to but the Canadian company did agree to a 25 per cent figure. When the people down there have you at a disadvantage you are apt to feel their boots. I am not suggesting that we ought to retaliate by putting the boots to the people of the United States. I am suggesting that this house should inform the National Energy Board that that board does not stand alone, and that this house is behind them when they walk down that hot, wide and sunny street in Vancouver to face the shooting. Incidentally, I hope it is sunny in Vancouver tomorrow.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I want the headlines in all Vancouver newspapers tomorrow to say that all parties in the House of Commons are united behind the board and that we are all united not only on the criteria set out in the royal commission's report but on the criteria set out in the National Energy Board Act.
When I asked the minister a question about this matter the other day he replied that he was sure the law would be enforced.
I am not so sure, Mr. Speaker. Of the last two contracts-and I am not speaking of the one involving the 27 cents starting price-the one where the National Energy Board agreed to 31 cents with the one cent escalating clause over a period of five years was close to the line in not keeping the law. The third agreement, however, breaks the law and goes against the recommendations of the royal commission.
I want the National Energy Board to have the assurance that, regardless of the party that forms the government, any Canadian government intends to back the law of Canada and that we intend to see that Canadian producers and Canadian consumers are treated equitably. That does not harm the citizens of the United States.
May I quote some figures. I think I remember them reasonably accurately. They show how the matter resolves itself into dollars and cents. What do the producers of gas in the San Juan valley get today for their gas? Here I am speaking of the alternative source for California and the northwest. Existing contracts for the New Mexico producers show that some get 45 cents per thousand
DEBATES	3375
Policy Statement on National Resources cubic feet at the well. In addition, there is a charge for shipping to the northwest. How do our producers in the Peace river area of British Columbia and Alberta fare? They get six cents, seven cents or eight cents; that is about their average. Why should we Canadians be asked to subsidize our main competitors in order to allow them to produce cheaper goods? There is no logic to this and any fairminded citizen of the United States knows that there is no logic here. Washington is waiting to see if we will stand up to be counted. Down there they have seen this government in the last few years wilting again and again. I have lots of evidence to show that there has been this wilting.
Before quoting figures may I read sections 83 (a) and (b) of the National Energy Board Act. These sections deal with the export and import of gas products. They read as follows:
83. Upon an application for a licence the Board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the Board shall satisfy itself that
(a)	the quantity of gas or power to be exported does not exceed the surplus remaining after due allowance has been made for the reasonably foreseeable requirements for use in Canada having regard to the trends in the discovery of gas in Canada;
Here we see the first principle. We must have a surplus of gas before any is exported. No one will argue that that condition has not been met. The Alberta Conservation Board looks after the Alberta interest and the National Energy Board of Canada looks after the Canadian interest. I wish to emphasize the importance of the following subsection:
(b)	the price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
In provisions relating to common carriers, and here I am speaking of oil pipe lines, and in the wording of the sections that deal with pricing policies, tolls and charges, existing legislation makes clear that discrimination must not be allowed to exist with respect to persons or localities. The only way to avoid discrimination is to charge consumers the lowest price at the well, and as the commodity goes across the country, whether to the east or west, the north or south, to charge a reasonable figure for transporting it. In that way each person is free to put into or take out of the pipe line the commodity with which he is concerned, knowing that the price charged for transmission will be fair. This is a fair principle in economics, but economics is not the only principle with

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of a national policy for Canadian resources is a subject of much greater importance than the attention which has been given to it would seem to warrant. During this centennial year we Canadians have been speaking a great deal about national identity, but even while we are speaking about national identity we are daily losing control of our own economy, and economic decisions affecting the lives of Canadian people are being taken out of the hands of Canadians and vested in the hands of corporations, mainly in the United States, which control the development of many of our resources.
We speak a great deal about being maitres chez nous, about being masters in our own house, but certainly there has been no clearly defined policy with respect to the utilization of Canadian resources which would guarantee that we are likely to continue to be masters of our own house or that we are even to any great extent masters in our own house at the present time. The whole development of the Canadian economy has been increasingly directed to making Canada a supplier of raw materials to the great industrial complex of the United States. We in Canada must face the fact, and face it fairly soon, that there are two schools of thought, the continentalist school and the nationalist school.
There are those who take a continental view of resources in the United States and Canada. They look upon these resources as having been pooled and see the vast resources of Canada as now being available to supply the United States which has depleted much of its own resources and is largely dependent upon Canada for oil, gas, minerals, lumber, and in some places even for water. Consequently this continental approach is being accepted not only by the Americans who have much to gain from it but also, unfortunately, by some Canadians as well.
This is an old imperial concept. It goes back to the days of the Romans. The whole idea of the Roman empire was to use Rome and the immediate environs of Italy as the centre of the empire and to use the peripheries of the empire, which stretched all the way from the British Isles to India, as areas from which to draw raw materials and manpower, to funnel these into the centre of the empire which produced manufactured products and then to sell them back to the colonial countries. The British Empire was built on the same idea.

In the nineteenth century particularly Britain built a great empire by developing a highly technical and industrial complex in the British Isles and by bringing raw materials from all parts of the great British Empire on which the sun never set. They developed at that time what was the most highly industrialized nation in the world. This, of course, was good for Britain, but it meant that the peripheral countries of the empire were little more than hewers of wood and drawers of water.
We are now witnessing the development of the great United States economic empire. The colonial concept is devised to make that kind of empire possible. The role which Canada would be assigned in such an empire would be to supply the raw materials and to supply materials, manpower and skilled professional people when the United States needs them. Canada would be expected to supply the raw materials which the people of the United States themselves have depleted in their own country and to help develop the United States so that it can continue to be what it is already, the greatest industrial and military power in the world.
I have no quarrel with the growth and development of the United States. But as a Canadian I think I have a responsibility to look at what a continental policy is likely to do to Canada. It would make Canada mainly a nation of extraction industries, a nation which would ship out its gas, oil, lumber and minerals, a nation which would sell its raw materials to the United States but which itself would continue to be underdeveloped and underemployed. We will never have in this country the kind of economic growth, the kind of full employment and the kind of parity of income which we desire until we adopt a nationalist Canadian policy with regard to the development of our resources.
When I speak of a nationalist policy I am not talking about a protectionist policy; I am talking about a policy in which the government ought to sit down and look at the whole question of what our resources are, how we can best use them and what apportionment of those resources will make for the greatest growth of the economy and the highest possible standards of living for the Canadian people.
If the government is to enunciate a resource policy I think the first thing it should do is determine how much of our resources are surplus to our needs, not only

Policy Statement on National Resources surplus to our needs at the moment but surplus to our needs in the foreseeable future. It should determine how much of our resources we need to retain in Canada to develop Canadian industry, how much of our resources can be processed or semi-processed in this country, and what resources we can afford to export in their raw state. When such an assessment is made I would certainly ask the government to keep in mind the following factors. The first is that nearly all the estimates which have been made to date concerning future economic requirements in respect of the load growth have been lamentably shortsighted. This has been true with reference to the consumption of oil, the consumption of gas and the utilization of electric power. All the estimates by the experts have been much too short. If we are to have estimates of what our requirements will be, those estimates ought to be very optimistic because I suspect that over the next 50 to 100 years our requirements for gas, oil, other energy materials and other basic raw materials will be much greater than anyone here foresees at the present time.
I think that the second thing which the government must keep in mind in working out an inventory of our requirements for the future is the fact that the resources we have today are part of the Canadian heritage. We are only the trustees of these resources; we have an obligation to conserve them and pass them on unimpaired to future generations. If we should allow our resources to be sold in a wild auction sale at fire sale prices we would be shortchanging the generations that follow.
I am not suggesting by that that we ought not to export any raw materials or any fuel, but I think Canadians of the present generation and certainly Canadians of future generations will hold us responsible if we do not ensure that an adequate and even more than adequate supply of the resources of Canada are retained in this country for the future economy of this country.
When we have determined what resources are surplus to our needs and what commodities we can allow to be exported, it seems to me the government must also lay down a very clear policy with regard to each of the commodities that we propose to export. Let us take oil which is one of the commodities that in all likelihood research will show we are likely to have in surplus supply. The fact that the tar sands can now be profitably developed opens up a whole new reservoir of oil, one of the largest reservoirs available in the world. This is a commodity which in all probability we will be able to export. Howev-

At that time I stated that we have the raw materials close at hand that could be processed into saleable products in the Atlantic area. I pointed out also that we have ports open the year round from which we could ship our goods by water, not only to other areas of Canada but to the markets of the world. I feel that too often we do not take advantage of what is available to us by way of our proximity to world markets.
I should like to stress that while the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve) did say some things that were controversial in his speech at Banff, he pointed out that we should expend our federal money in an effort to produce a deep-water port in the strait of Canso area which would take advantage of the growing industrial complex there. Certainly I would be the first to encourage him in this regard. I should like also to see the federal government do everything possible to modernize the ports of Halifax and Saint John so that we would not be slipping behind, but would be going forward in our endeavours to provide the best facilities available to the shipping companies of the world.
I believe we are strategically located in Atlantic Canada to take full advantage of the concessions we have acquired under the Kennedy round, and if our ports were as modem and as efficient as they might be with a realistic government program we would then be in a better position to take full advantage of what might be available as a result of the Kennedy round negotiations. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) mentioned that there was only one company other than Dosco that might possibly be interested in controlling and utilizing the facilities
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Tardif).]
at Sydney, Nova Scotia. I feel he should examine the facts as they exist today. He would learn that there is a wholly owned Canadian company, I believe, which has indicated it is anxious to acquire Dosco holdings not only in the maritime provinces but also in the province of Quebec. One of the main points made by this company in its submission to the government of Canada and the government of Nova Scotia relates to water transportation and the accessibility to foreign markets. They feel that they could take the steel complex at Sydney and Con-trecoeur and make it into a going concern. Naturally it is my hope, and I am sure the hope of the people of Nova Scotia, that this company has the kind of resources available that will allow it to secure control and allow it to utilize the cornerstone industry that exists there now, without which the whole economy of the area would be jeopardized.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I think members in all parts of the house should take cognizance of the facts pointed out in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of October 18, that a great many taxpayers' dollars have been expended on certain government projects that were beneficial to the whole nation, even though the return from them at any given time may not have been apparent. I am sure that the St. Lawrence Seaway, which has cost the Canadian taxpayer in excess of $400 million, would qualify, as would I feel certain the sum expended on the Avro Arrow, a project which was never completed but which cost the taxpayer $341 million. Nova Scotians did not berate the government of Canada for entering into such a project or for spending such a vast amount of money.

I am sure I could point to many more examples of industries in various parts of the nation having to be maintained for the good of the economy of Canada.
This is the situation that obtains in the Atlantic area today. If the government and the minister would do everything in their power to see that the committee that is studying the potential of the Bay of Fundy tides produces its report before 1969, which is now

the target date, I think we could move in the direction of producing results which would end our problems. If the project that is under way were to receive the kind of endorsement that I believe it will receive, then surely the expenditure of the millions of dollars that would be demanded would very quickly restore confidence in the minds of the people of this area. With respect to our gas policy I have already indicated the growth which has taken place in recent years, and have given a reassurance to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam about the future of that industry in terms of maintaining availability for Canadian development.
This afternoon mention was made of the role of the National Energy Board. I might not call what was said criticism, but certainly suggestions were made with respect to the board and its operations.
The gas policy of the government is to be found mainly in the National Energy Board Act, and with respect to prices is clearly defined in section 83 which reads:
Upon an application tor a licence the board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the board shall satisfy itself that
(a)	the quantity of gas or power to be exported does not exceed the surplus remaining after due allowance has been made for the reasonably foreseeable requirements for use in Canada having regard to the trends in the discovery of gas in Canada; and
(b)	the price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
This afternoon we were asked what the national gas policy was. It is given there. It is the responsibility of the National Energy Board to assess if the export quantities and the export prices are acceptable or not in the Canadian interest. This is not done in a back room; it is done at public hearings. Anybody can attend those hearings. For example, if the government of British Columbia has fears about the future of gas supplies in their province and about deliveries of gas in British Columbia, it can send a representative to appear before the board hearings in Vancouver, and say so. This is all done in public. No shadows cover the subject. In addition, after finding out the facts the board has to produce a written report of possibly 100 or 200 pages explaining the why's, the when's and the how's of the decisions it makes.
The board's report is not a private document. From it the public can make a judgment, and if the board makes a judgment favourable to an applicant the government of
DEBATES	3399
Policy Statement on National Resources Canada has to acquiesce in that decision. Then, as in the case of the Great Lakes transmission pipe line, the government must accept responsibility for its decision. If hon. members are not pleased with the government's decision they can criticize it, seek a special debate, and do whatever they want in order to bring it to the attention of the world.
In the light of these facts I am still a bit curious about the kind of changes my hon. friends opposite would like to bring about.
With respect to prices I could give a full explanation on the way in which prices are assessed by the National Energy Board. It follows a number of criteria which practice has taught it are reliable ones. It makes a comparison with the price of similar sales of gas at adjacent points in Canada. A second criterion involves a comparison with the price of similar exports. A third is a comparison with similar purchases from sources in the United States. Fourth, the board assesses the difference between price and costs. After all these considerations and others the board makes a decision.
I do not want to go into too much detail on this matter, but there are a number of systems of pricing. For example there is the "cost of service" basis, and the "straight contract" basis.
In the case of Westcoast Transmission the straight contract approach has created a problem. A contract was entered into in 1956 for certain quantities of gas at a price of 22 cents per thousand cubic feet. The answer given by the Department of Fisheries mentions the Fisheries Research Board. The Department of Forestry and Rural Development tells us:
The Forestry Branch is indirectly concerned with one aspect of stream pollution, as an extension of its programs of research on the chemical control of forest defoliators, and through co-operative studies with the Fisheries Department to develop aerial spray formulations that present minimal hazards to aquatic fauna.
The Department of National Health and Welfare says there are two divisions of the department which are involved in the study and/or control of fresh water pollution, use or disposition.
Oddly enough, in answer to the question whether there is a cabinet committee dealing with the subject-a question to which the department of mines and technical surveys had answered, yes-the Department of National Health and Welfare said, no. Perhaps this is another indication that the minister responsible for this department does not know what is going on. The reply given is:
No. However, an advisory committee on water use policy was constituted in 1959 composed of deputy ministers of various government departments.
The Department of Agriculture mentions the prairie farm rehabilitation administration. The Department of Industry answers that the National Research Council is engaged in scientific and engineering research activities the results of which might be of interest in the study or control of pollution of water. Mention is made of the associate committee on water pollution research, the associate committee on waves and littoral drift and the Canadian national committee for the international hydrologic decade.
Next we find the department of northern affairs and national resources replying as follows:
The Canadian Wildlife Service is engaged in the study of fresh-water pollution resulting from the use of pesticides and biocides.. . and is also engaged in the study of use of fresh-water as it relates to the management of the migratory bird resource throughout Canada and to sport fish in the National parks of Canada.
Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, minister of transport at that time, answered that the Atlantic Development Board was responsible for some activities in the field of water control.

About the same time as this inquiry was made I myself put a question on the order paper and received a similar answer from the various departments through the secretary of state; the replies were more or less parallel to those given in answer to the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). The answer I received was more specific with respect to activities in the field of pollution control. However, it gave the same impression that there was a sporadic, scattered, fragmented approach to the problem of pollution; that responsibility for study and action was scattered among various departments and agencies of the federal government and that there were a few thousand dollars scattered here and there throughout the estimates for work related, directly or indirectly, to the study, control and reduction of pollution.
The question we want answered is whether the situation today is any different from the situation which existed in March, 1966. As far as I know, no statement has been forthcoming to indicate that there has been any change from that scattered, hodge-podge miscellaneous effort. The hon. member for Burna-by-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka raised the question of federal legislative control. My leader mentioned section 165 of the Criminal Code which makes the creation of a nuisance endangering health, life, safety and so on an offence. In addition, of course, we have the federal Fisheries Act. Perhaps I should read to the house section 61 of that act. This particular section is, of course, concerned only with fish, and states:
Every person who causes or knowingly permits to pass into, or puts or knowingly permits to be put, lime, chemical substances or drugs, poisonous matter, dead or decaying fish, or remnants thereof, mill rubbish or sawdust or any other deleterious substance or thing, whether the same is of the like character to the substances named in this section or not, in any water frequented by fish, is liable, for the first offence, to a penalty of twenty dollars and costs, for the second offence to a penalty of not less than forty dollars and costs, and not more than eighty dollars and costs, and also in addition thereto a further penalty of not less than ten dollars and not more than twenty dollars for every day during which such offence is continued; and for the third or any subsequent offence, to a penalty of not less than one hundred dollars and costs, and not more than two hundred dollars and costs, and also in addition thereto a further penalty not exceeding twenty dollars for every day during which such offence is continued.
It is doubtful whether these punitive or restrictive pieces of legislation are really the answer; the emphasis is not placed, in the main, where I believe most hon. members of this house feel it should be placed. I agree

Mr. Speaker, the two-concept philosophy of the Conservative party is an historic fact.
In 1911, the Quebec ultra-nationalist elements joined with the Imperialists, and the famous conscription which was highly denounced later on in the province of Quebec, resulted from that combination. A little later, in 1940-1945, Mr. Bracken's draft promoters joined with some so-called independents who came on the Quebec scene, the same ones who had also highly denounced Canadian participation in the world war.
Some time later, that same Conservative party-all this to prove its doctrinal hybridity-had in its bosom people like Jean-Noel Tremblay, an avowed separatist, who joined a John Diefenbaker who has always repudiated the two-nation concept.
At the last Conservative convention, Mr. Speaker, the famous two-nation concept became the war-cry of the Conservative party. Once again, the doctrinal hybridity of the party is manifest.
Now, what trick did the adoption of that stand hide? This subterfuge: that ideological deception, that political cant, was nothing but a wish or an attempt to live in concubinage with Daniel Johnson's Union Nationale. Now, Mr. Johnson was not taken in by that, because if the two-nation concept is to be implemented, it means, first of all, that we need a new constitution.

The two-nation concept also implies statehood for a nation, the French-Canadian nation then having the right to identify itself with its own state. Another circumstance which makes the offence even more serious, Mr. Speaker, is that he spoke at a meeting of the International Conference of the Financial Executives Institute.
Another aggravating circumstance, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that he attacks, that he takes for his target the lawful government, a government elected according to the rules of democracy, and responsible for the country's future; this government should be far more conscientious than this citizen would have us believe.
